title: Molecular Results in Context: FISH, Leukaemia Genetics, CFTR and SNPs
summary: Learn why molecular results are read with morphology, how FISH shows translocations, rearrangements and deletions, how genetics subtypes leukaemias, why two CFTR variants do not by themselves mean cystic fibrosis, and what the one-SNP-per-1000-bases figure really means.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 67 Hits 1, 4, 5, 13 and 14 and Exam Trap 1. Checked against the WHO 5th edition myeloid (Khoury 2022) and lymphoid (Alaggio 2022) papers, Cui 2016 (FISH), the Brazilian APL consensus (de Figueiredo-Pontes 2024), the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation 2008 consensus (Farrell 2008; read via a page-fetch tool, first ~100,000 characters), Esposito 2020, Bell 2002, Hoehe 2004 and the 1000 Genomes 2015 paper. The reviewer’s “~1 SNP per 1000 bp” is kept as the classic approximation with context; the reviewer’s “CFTR expanded cystic fibrosis to milder forms” is taught with the guideline label CFTR-related disorder. The 2017 CF Foundation update was not read. Not taught: the list of molecular methods in Hit 1, SNP use in parentage/forensics, Trap 1’s wrong-cells/contamination example, and the US CPT/billing Hits.

objectives: Explain why a molecular result is interpreted with morphology and the clinical picture, using clonal haematopoiesis as an example.
Describe how FISH shows translocations, gene rearrangements and deletions, and why interphase FISH is rapid.
Distinguish cystic fibrosis from a CFTR-related disorder and put the one-SNP-per-1000-bp figure in context.

scenes.title: Three molecular results, three contexts
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three molecular results reach the laboratory. (1) A 72-year-old with normal blood counts and no blood disorder: a mutation in a myeloid-malignancy-associated gene at a variant allele fraction of 3%. (2) A bone marrow full of abnormal promyelocytes: the clinician needs to know about PML::RARA today. (3) A 30-year-old man with infertility from congenital absence of the vas deferens, normal lungs and pancreas, sweat chloride in the normal range: two CFTR variants. Question token: “What does each result actually mean?”

cues.text: Three molecular results arrive. A healthy seventy-two-year-old with normal blood counts carries a myeloid gene mutation at three percent.
A marrow full of abnormal promyelocytes needs a PML RARA answer today.
And an infertile man with absent vas deferens, healthy lungs and pancreas, carries two CFTR variants with a normal sweat test. What does each result actually mean?

props.label: What does each result actually mean?

scenes.title: Genes and morphology together
scenes.altText: Schematic: four cards based on the WHO 5th edition haematolymphoid classification (2022). Integration card: the classification is applied by integrating morphology (cytology and histology), immunophenotype, molecular and cytogenetic data. B-ALL card: B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma can be diagnosed at the class level on morphology and immunophenotype alone, but most subtypes are defined by ploidy changes (hyperdiploidy, hypodiploidy) or chromosomal rearrangements such as ETV6::RUNX1 and BCR::ABL1. AML card: acute myeloid leukaemias with defining genetic abnormalities (for example acute promyelocytic leukaemia with PML::RARA) no longer need 20% blasts, except AML with BCR::ABL1 and with CEBPA mutation. Correlation card: removing the blast cutoff requires correlating morphology with the molecular findings to make sure the abnormality is driving the disease.

cues.text: Leukaemia classification shows how much molecular testing now matters. The 2022 WHO classification is applied by putting together morphology, immunophenotype, molecular and cytogenetic results.

Morphology and immunophenotype alone can call a case B-lymphoblastic leukaemia. Telling its subtypes apart takes genetics: chromosome number changes, and rearrangements such as ETV6 RUNX1 or BCR ABL1.
In acute myeloid leukaemia, most types with a defining genetic change, such as acute promyelocytic leukaemia with PML RARA, no longer need twenty percent blasts.
But the classification warns that this needs correlation: morphology and molecular findings must agree that the abnormality is really driving the disease.

scenes.title: How FISH sees rearrangements and deletions
scenes.altText: Schematic nucleus with coloured dots. Principle card (Cui et al., 2016): fluorescent DNA probes hybridise to complementary sequences in fixed cells or tissue and are viewed under a fluorescence microscope; resolution about 100–200 kb, set by probe size, versus 5–10 Mb for high-resolution G-banding. Interphase card: FISH works on non-dividing (interphase) nuclei, so no cell culture is needed and results are rapid. Probe card: dual-colour double-fusion probes show a reciprocal translocation as fused signals (for example BCR::ABL1); break-apart probes show a rearranged gene as split signals; a microdeletion shows as loss of one signal. Urgent card: in acute promyelocytic leukaemia, FISH for PML::RARA can give a result within hours (under 24 h; Brazilian consensus 2024), while all-trans retinoic acid is started as soon as APL is suspected, without waiting for the result; karyotyping follows to show the full clone.

cues.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridisation, FISH, uses fluorescent probes that stick to matching DNA in fixed cells. It resolves about one to two hundred kilobases, far finer than the five to ten megabases of banded chromosomes.
It works on interphase nuclei, cells that are not dividing, so there is no culture step and the answer comes quickly.
Probe design reveals the change. Two colours that fuse mark a translocation such as BCR ABL1. A break-apart probe that splits marks a rearranged gene. And a missing signal marks a deletion.
In acute promyelocytic leukaemia, PML RARA FISH can answer within hours, but all-trans retinoic acid starts as soon as the disease is suspected. A karyotype then shows the whole clone.

props.title: APL: rapid PML::RARA FISH
lines: Result in hours · ATRA starts on suspicion

scenes.title: CFTR spectrum, SNP density, hook answers
scenes.altText: CFTR card (Cystic Fibrosis Foundation consensus, Farrell et al., 2008): CFTR mutations cause a spectrum from sinusitis in adulthood to severe lung, pancreatic or liver disease in infancy; the sweat chloride test is the primary confirmatory test; CF cannot be diagnosed simply by finding two CFTR mutations, which must be CF-causing and fit the clinical picture; partial or single-organ phenotypes (for example congenital absence of the vas deferens, recurrent or chronic pancreatitis, bronchiectasis) in people with CFTR mutations who do not meet CF criteria are labelled CFTR-related disorders, and some may later meet CF criteria. A 2020 study found undiagnosed CFTR-related disorders in some CF carriers after extended CFTR analysis. SNP card: SNP frequency of approximately 1 per 1000 base pairs (Bell, 2002); resequencing of genes across many people found about one SNP every 185 bp (Hoehe and Kroslak, 2004); a typical genome differs from the reference at 4.1–5.0 million sites, over 99.9% being SNPs and short indels (1000 Genomes, 2015). Hook answers: (1) CHIP, not leukaemia; (2) rapid interphase FISH for PML::RARA; (3) CFTR-related disorder, not classic CF.

cues.text: CFTR variants cause a spectrum of disease. A sweat chloride test confirms CF, and two CFTR variants alone do not make the diagnosis. Single-organ disease, such as absent vas deferens or recurrent pancreatitis, that does not meet CF criteria is called a CFTR-related disorder.

SNPs are the commonest variant: roughly one per thousand bases is the classic figure. Gene surveys across many people find them denser, and a typical genome differs from the reference at four to five million sites.

Back to the hook. The healthy seventy-two-year-old has clonal haematopoiesis, not leukaemia. The promyelocytes need rapid FISH for PML RARA. And the man with absent vas deferens fits a CFTR-related disorder, not classic cystic fibrosis.

props.title: CFTR: a spectrum
lines: Single organ, no CF criteria → CFTR-RD

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A positive molecular result is the diagnosis” (✓ CHIP is a myeloid-gene mutation in blood at VAF ≥2% in a person without a diagnosed blood disorder or unexplained cytopenia; molecular findings are correlated with morphology); “Two CFTR variants = cystic fibrosis” (✓ CF cannot be diagnosed simply by two mutations; sweat chloride, clinical features and whether the variants are CF-causing decide, and single-organ disease short of CF criteria is a CFTR-related disorder); “SNPs occur exactly once every 1000 bases” (✓ an approximation; density depends on what is compared).

cues.text: Trap one: a positive molecular result is the diagnosis. No: a myeloid mutation in a person with no blood disorder is clonal haematopoiesis, and molecular findings are read with morphology.
Trap two: two CFTR variants mean cystic fibrosis. No: sweat chloride and clinical features decide, and single-organ disease that falls short of CF criteria is a CFTR-related disorder.
Trap three: SNPs fall exactly every thousand bases. No: that is an approximation, and the density depends on what you compare.

props.title: ✗ “Two CFTR variants = CF.”
lines: ✓ Sweat chloride + clinical picture; else CFTR-RD

scenes.title: Map and window
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “The molecular result is the MAP; morphology and the clinical picture are the WINDOW. Check the window before you trust the map.” Tokens: Map = gene result · Window = cells and patient · Agree = diagnosis. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the molecular result is the map, and morphology and the patient are the window. Look out of the window before you trust the map.
Where it breaks: for many leukaemias the genetic change now defines the type; FISH sees only what its probes target; and CHIP is a real precursor state, not a false result.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Molecular + morphology together · FISH finds fusions, splits and deletions”, “Two CFTR variants, single-organ disease, no CF criteria → CFTR-related disorder · 1 SNP per 1000 bp is approximate”.

cues.text: Molecular results work in context, so FISH and genetic subtyping classify leukaemias alongside morphology, single-organ disease with two CFTR variants that falls short of cystic fibrosis criteria is a CFTR-related disorder, and one SNP per thousand bases is only an approximation.

explanation.what: Plain language: a gene test can say a change is present, but not by itself whether it is causing disease. Doctors put the gene result together with what the cells look like and how the patient is. Scientific terms: WHO 5th edition haematolymphoid classification, defining genetic abnormality, clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), variant allele fraction (VAF), fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH), interphase FISH, dual-colour double-fusion and break-apart probes, sweat chloride test, CFTR-related disorder (CFTR-RD), single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP).
explanation.why: Molecular tests detect specific sequences very sensitively, so a finding can be real but clinically different from what it seems (a precursor clone, a mild single-organ CFTR disorder). Leukaemia classification now relies on genetics for subtyping, which makes correlation with morphology more important, not less.
explanation.measure: Sweat chloride (Farrell 2008, over 6 months of age): ≤39 mmol/L CF unlikely, 40–59 intermediate, ≥60 indicative of CF. CHIP: myeloid-malignancy-associated mutation at VAF ≥2% (≥4% for X-linked genes in males) without a diagnosed blood disorder or unexplained cytopenia. FISH resolution ~100–200 kb vs 5–10 Mb for high-resolution banding. AML with defining genetic abnormalities: no 20% blast requirement, except BCR::ABL1 and CEBPA-mutated AML. SNPs: classic ~1 per 1000 bp; gene resequencing across people ~1 per 185 bp; typical genome vs reference 4.1–5.0 million differing sites.
explanation.differs: FISH (targeted, interphase, fast, ~100–200 kb) vs karyotype (whole-genome view of the clone, metaphases, 5–10 Mb); CF (sweat chloride and characteristic clinical features, with CF-causing variants) vs CFTR-related disorder (single-organ or partial disease with CFTR variants that does not meet CF criteria); CHIP vs myeloid neoplasm.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: a positive molecular result with normal morphology (does it replace the diagnosis?), which FISH pattern shows a translocation or deletion, why FISH is used for urgent APL, how a man with CBAVD and CFTR variants is classified, and the approximate SNP frequency.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with normal blood counts and no blood disorder has a mutation in a myeloid-malignancy-associated gene at a variant allele fraction of 3% in peripheral blood. Which description fits best under the WHO 2022 classification?

options.rationale: Correct. CHIP is defined as such a mutation at VAF ≥2% in a person without a diagnosed blood disorder or unexplained cytopenia.
Incorrect. A mutation alone, with normal counts, does not make leukaemia; molecular findings are correlated with morphology.
Incorrect. MDS is defined by cytopenias and morphologic dysplasia, which are absent here.

options.text: A laboratory error that should be reported as negative
options.rationale: Incorrect. CHIP is a recognised, real finding, not by itself a sign of error.

questions.stem: A marrow suggests acute promyelocytic leukaemia and a PML::RARA answer is needed urgently. Why is FISH on interphase nuclei suited to this?

options.text: It needs no cell culture, so a targeted fusion result is available rapidly
options.rationale: Correct. Interphase FISH avoids the culture step and can give a PML::RARA result within hours; all-trans retinoic acid itself is started as soon as APL is suspected, without waiting for the result.

options.text: It requires dividing cells, which APL marrows provide in abundance
options.rationale: Incorrect. Interphase FISH works on non-dividing nuclei; karyotyping is the method that needs metaphases.

options.text: Its resolution of 5–10 Mb shows the whole genome at once
options.rationale: Incorrect. 5–10 Mb is the resolution of high-resolution banding; FISH resolves ~100–200 kb but only at its probe targets.

options.text: It sequences every base of the fusion gene
options.rationale: Incorrect. FISH detects probe hybridisation signals, not the base sequence.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has infertility from congenital absence of the vas deferens, no lung or pancreatic disease, a normal sweat chloride (below 40 mmol/L) on repeat testing, and two CFTR variants. Under the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation consensus, how is he best classified?

options.rationale: Correct. Single-organ disease with CFTR variants that does not meet CF criteria is labelled a CFTR-related disorder; a sweat chloride of 39 mmol/L or less after 6 months of age is generally not consistent with CF.

options.text: Cystic fibrosis, because two CFTR variants are present
options.rationale: Incorrect. The consensus states CF cannot be diagnosed simply by finding two CFTR mutations; sweat chloride and clinical features decide, and his sweat chloride is normal.

options.text: Unrelated to CFTR, because his lungs are normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. Absence of the vas deferens is a recognised CFTR-related single-organ presentation.
Incorrect. He has two variants plus a CFTR-related clinical finding, which is more than carrier status.

claims.text: Molecular results are integrated with morphology, immunophenotype and cytogenetics; genetically defined AML types require morphology–molecular correlation; CHIP definition.
Genetics subtypes leukaemias: B-ALL subtypes by ploidy and rearrangements; AML with defining genetic abnormalities including APL with PML::RARA without a 20% blast cutoff (except BCR::ABL1, CEBPA).
FISH principle, resolution, interphase use, fusion/break-apart/lost-signal patterns, rapid PML::RARA FISH in APL (result within hours; ATRA started on suspicion); karyotype for the whole clone.
CFTR spectrum; sweat chloride confirms CF (cut-offs 39/40–59/60 mmol/L after 6 months); two mutations alone do not diagnose CF; single-organ disease short of CF criteria is a CFTR-related disorder.
claims.note: Based on the 2008 consensus; the 2017 update was not read.

claims.text: SNP frequency ~1 per 1000 bp (classic approximation); ~1 per 185 bp in gene resequencing across people; typical genome vs reference 4.1–5.0 million sites.

Hit 1 definition (hybridisation, amplification, sequencing, microarrays for diagnosis, prognosis, therapy selection and monitoring); SNP use in parentage and forensics; Trap 1 example of a positive signal from contaminating DNA or a sample without tumour.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 67 Hit 4 gives ~1 SNP per 1000 bp as a fixed rate. Bell 2002 gives the same approximation, but gene resequencing across many people found about one SNP every 185 bp (Hoehe 2004), and a typical genome differs from the reference at 4.1–5.0 million sites (1000 Genomes 2015); the figure depends on what is compared. The lesson teaches ~1/1000 as an approximation with that context (register flag rv-ch67-snp-rate-context).

Ch. 67 Hit 14 says CFTR analysis expanded cystic fibrosis to milder/atypical forms such as CBAVD and chronic pancreatitis. The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation consensus (Farrell 2008) classifies such single-organ presentations as CFTR-related disorders, states that CF cannot be diagnosed simply by two CFTR mutations, keeps sweat chloride as the primary confirmatory test, and notes some such patients may later meet CF criteria; the lesson teaches that distinction (register flag rv-ch67-cftr-related-disorder).
